title: Fox Army Health Center shares update on flu vaccine | News | theredstonerocket.com
description: Fox Army Health Center is increasing warfighter readiness again this quarter through a flu shot campaign that began in late September.
text:
As the community settles into fall, the Top of Alabama Regional Council of Gover…

Who is your hero and why?



Fox Army Health Center is increasing warfighter readiness again this quarter through a flu shot campaign that began in late September.

The campaign comes after Secretary of War Pete Hegseth stated that the flu vaccine is optional for the armed forces. The policy has been in place since 1945 and saw another brief rescinding in 1949.

“Our men and women in uniform were forced to choose between their conscience and their country. Even when those decisions posed no threat to our military readiness. You know what I’m talking about, what happened during COVID-19,” Hegseth said during a video statement posted to the social media platform X in April. “No more; that era of betrayal is over. … We’re seizing this moment to discard any absurd, overreaching mandates that only weaken our warfighting capabilities.”

However, a flu outbreak in the Air Force led to their reinstatement of the mandate in July, which subsequently led to the reinstatement of the policy for the Navy and Marines.

For Redstone Arsenal, flu vaccination is mandatory for those assigned to or participating in basic training, forces preparing for deployment, immediate response force service members, first responders, Army personnel working in a medical unit, confinement inmates and staff and Child and Youth Services staff.

“This campaign will be available for all Tricare beneficiaries,” Lt. Col. Aimee Mack, commander of Fox Army Health Center, said.

Mack said appointments can be made and that walk-ins are welcome. Hours for the shots are 8 a.m. to noon and then 1-3 p.m. On Oct. 23, during Retiree Appreciation Day, attendees can expect Fox to be present with the vaccine for their Retiree Appreciation Day flu drive.

She also said that if a team or group of people are looking to get flu shots done simultaneously, they can reach out to the health center. “Scheduling will be done and we’ll send over a team to get your group shots done.”

Mack said Fox accepts outside X-ray orders, also for those with Tricare insurance. However, it is important to note that X-rays are the only radiology service currently available at Fox.

“If you have a written X-ray order, we can complete them here at Fox, our radiology department would be glad to schedule it,” she said.

Those interested in scheduling an appointment can call 256-955-8888. Mack also mentioned that there has been an abundance of no shows, and since the health center is short-staffed, cancellations in advance are encouraged.

The same number can be dialed to cancel, with extension 2 being pressed if the call is during the normal hours of operation, or extension 3 for after hours and weekends.

text:
Disconnect to farms

The content of Monday's newspaper is rather exemplary of the lack of consistent reporting on agricultural economic issues in Arkansas. Agriculture is seemingly the largest driver of Arkansas' economy. But Monday there was not one significant article about the agricultural businesses.

So when this newspaper wails about declining subscriptions with likely three-fourths of the citizens having some relationship or attachment to the rural farming community, it is not surprising that the print media such as this one fails to thrive.

Could there possibly be an a-ha moment? Take the Democrat-Gazette team on a weekend retreat to a working farm and get some dirt between your fingers and toes so they can understand where agricultural produce and food is manufactured. And then report on it.

THOMAS J. ALSTON

Texarkana

Veterans' medicines

On April 16, 2025, the General Assembly of Arkansas approved, and Gov. Sarah Sanders signed, Act 624, which effectively denies active-duty service members and their families, and retired military personnel including reserve component retirees and their families, the right to use one of the benefits given to us by the U.S. Congress, that of receiving our prescription medications by mail through Express Scripts, the Department of Defense TRICARE selected provider.

The law that was passed requires the state pharmacy board to revoke the license of pharmacies that have Pharmacy Benefit Managers (PBM) outside Arkansas. PBMs deal with negotiations and payments throughout the supply chain. This was done, at the request of the pharmacy lobby, to force the above-mentioned personnel to purchase their medications at local pharmacies or obtain them from one of the three VA pharmacies located in Arkansas. All three are in the Little Rock area. The end result will be that in order to use the pharmacy benefit, veterans will have to make long trips. Many are disabled and will have to have someone assist them for the up to 400-mile round trip. It is not likely that the three pharmacies can adequately accommodate the 182,000 veterans who live in Arkansas.

After this law was made public, both Express Scripts and CVS, the other entity affected, filed lawsuits against the state. U.S. District Judge Brian Miller issued a preliminary injunction against the act. The state immediately challenged the ruling. The case continues in the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Arkansas. A recent check of their website shows that it is still an active case.

Upon realizing the implications of this act, I contacted Governor Sanders' office, hoping that she would come to the aid of the veterans of Arkansas. No acknowledgment, no response. I further contacted the office of Sen. Tom Cotton, a fellow veteran, asking for his assistance. No acknowledgment, no response.

The midterm elections are coming soon. Guess for whom I will not vote.

HAROLD JOHNSON

Arkadelphia

Artificial intelligence

Surely I am not the first person to predict a war between AI companies. Is competitive nature inherent in AI? What would happen in such a war?

CHARLIE BISHOP

Mabelvale

Mocking of humans

As a 69-year-old resident of Hot Springs Village, I recently registered as an unaffiliated voter in Arkansas. For nearly 45 years, I was a registered Republican and conservative voter; I couldn't count on one hand the number of Democratic candidates I've ever voted for.

Recently, however, Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders has pushed me even further away from the Republican Party through her recent political advertisements concerning welfare and transgender policy initiatives.

To be clear, I am not opposed to reasonable work requirements for able-bodied welfare recipients, nor am I opposed to athletics department policies restricting biological males from participating in girls' sports. What I strongly oppose is the governor's decision to air ads that actively mock human beings--those who are less fortunate than her, and those who are struggling to find their way in this world with sexual identity issues.

Governor Sanders, I assume, considers herself a faithful evangelical Christian committed to spreading the Gospel. Yet Jesus plainly taught in the Sermon on the Mount: "Judge not, that ye be not judged." The governor's advertisements run completely contrary to her profession of faith and represent an endorsement of the ugly, divisive politics currently cursing our culture.

These ads are not "Making America Great Again"--they are simply making us look cruel and unkind. I hope the governor reads this letter and helps me understand: How can she reconcile these advertisements with a life lived as a follower of Christ?

BOB GREGG

Hot Springs Village

title: $26 Million TRICARE Scam Bought a Gold-Plated Cybertruck - Popsmokemedia
description:

The clinics billed TRICARE more than $26 million for transcranial magnetic stimulation, or TMS, therapy.

text:
For active-duty troops, veterans and military families, the money was supposed to pay for healthcare. Instead, prosecutors say it helped fund a luxury lifestyle.

Kevin D. Curry, 64, of Frisco, Texas, was convicted by a federal jury on September 24 after prosecutors accused him of running a sprawling healthcare fraud, kickback and money-laundering scheme through three mental health clinics in Texas and Florida. The Justice Department announced the conviction on September 25.

Between September 2022 and December 2025, Curry operated Acuity TMS clinics in Plano and Fort Worth, Texas, and Emerald Coast TMS in Fort Walton Beach, Florida. The locations were close to major military communities, including Eglin Air Force Base, Hurlburt Field and Naval Air Station Joint Reserve Base Fort Worth.

The clinics billed TRICARE more than $26 million for transcranial magnetic stimulation, or TMS, therapy. According to prosecutors, some treatments were medically unnecessary, some were never provided and others involved patients who did not qualify.

TRICARE ultimately paid about $17 million.

Prosecutors said Curry went even further. He allegedly offered and paid more than $5.5 million in illegal kickbacks to persuade active-duty service members, veterans and their family members to agree to treatments. Employees were also directed to fabricate medical records, while Curry allegedly used doctors’ credentials without their knowledge to support fraudulent claims.

Then came the spending.

Federal prosecutors said Curry used some of the money for luxury hotel stays, a lavish casino-themed party and a gold-plated Tesla Cybertruck valued at more than $100,000. Federal authorities seized the Cybertruck in January along with other assets connected to the case.

The case became a joint investigation involving the Defense Criminal Investigative Service, FBI, Texas Medicaid Fraud Control Unit and the Department of Veterans Affairs Office of Inspector General.

The jury ultimately convicted Curry on three counts of healthcare fraud, three counts involving illegal healthcare kickbacks and three counts involving transactions with criminally derived property.

He has not yet been sentenced.

Curry faces a maximum of 10 years in federal prison on each of the nine counts, although his eventual sentence will be determined by a federal judge under federal sentencing rules.

The strange image of a gold Cybertruck may be what makes the case go viral. But behind it is a much more serious question: how did millions of dollars intended for the healthcare of America's military community end up financing luxury spending?

For the troops, veterans and families whose care was allegedly used to generate the money, the gold truck is more than an outrageous purchase. It is the most visible symbol of where the prosecutors say the money went.

Editor’s Note: Curry was convicted by a federal jury and is presumed innocent of any charges for which he was not convicted. The allegations described above are based on evidence presented at trial and statements from the U.S. Department of Justice. Curry is scheduled to be sentenced at a later date.

description:

The benefit will cover up to $500 a year in sperm cryopreservation costs.

text:
Genito-urological Injuries Increased in Warfighters After 2001

WASHINGTON — Nearly 2,000 U.S. troops suffered debilitating injuries to their groins or genitals during the wars in Iraq and Afghanistan between 2000 and 2013, and about 307,000 more sustained some type of head injury over the same period, all injuries that can compromise fertility and sexual function. Those figures illustrate the stakes behind family-planning decisions made ahead of a combat deployment and motivate a new Pentagon program that will help troops preserve before they deploy their ability to have children.

A notice published in the Federal Register on Aug. 13 announced that the DoD will launch a 3-year demonstration project on Sept. 14 that reimburses eligible active-duty servicemembers for the cost of freezing sperm or eggs. The benefit will cover up to $500 a year in sperm cryopreservation costs. The reimbursement rises to $10,000 a year for egg, or oocyte, cryopreservation, reflecting the far higher cost and complexity of egg retrieval, which typically requires hormone stimulation and a surgical procedure, compared with sperm banking.

The program, required by Section 709 of the Servicemember Quality of Life Improvement and National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2025, is open to active-duty members of the Army, Navy, Marine Corps, Air Force and Space Force who meet at least one of three conditions. These include receiving orders for an assignment that qualifies for hazardous duty pay, being likely to receive such orders within 120 days or being separated from a spouse, domestic partner or dating partner for 180 days or more under orders, including sea duty.

Participation is voluntary. Eligible troops can obtain preservation services either at a military treatment facility with a reproductive medicine program or through a civilian clinic of their choosing. Reimbursable costs include gamete retrieval procedures and the medications and lab testing associated with them, cryopreservation itself and the shipping and storage of the samples for the duration of the 3-year demonstration.

Because the Defense Health Agency does not have visibility into deployment orders, commanders must validate a servicemember’s eligibility before reimbursement is approved. Troops must submit a complete DHA Form 459, along with itemized invoices, within 120 days of the date services began, typically the date of retrieval or the associated lab procedure or prescription. Servicemembers could be eligible for reimbursement more than once during the 3-year pilot, if they again meet the eligibility criteria.

Participants also will be required to attest that they have an advance medical directive specifying what should happen to their preserved gametes in the event of their death. Decisions about continued storage, disposition or future use after the demonstration period remain solely the responsibility of the servicemember and fall outside the scope of the program, according to the notice.

The program has been more than a decade in coming. In 2016, then-Defense Secretary Ash Carter announced a similar pilot as part of a broader package of family-friendly policies, saying the department wanted to help troops preserve their ability to start a family even after a combat injury. That earlier program never got off the ground. This time, the effort comes with a congressional mandate and a defined evaluation plan: The Pentagon will track how many servicemembers use the benefit, its total cost, the administrative burden of running it and its effects on force readiness, retention and member satisfaction during the pilot period.

Military families and support organizations have pushed for such benefits for years. Improvised explosive devices (IEDs) were the signature weapon of the wars in Iraq and Afghanistan, causing thousands of severe combat casualties and complex, multi-system trauma. Among the most devastating were urotrauma and pelvic injuries. Severe blast winds and ground-strike detonations caused devastating damage to the pelvis, urinary tract, and reproductive organs.

In a 2023 study, a Rutgers University research team used predefined search criteria to primarily identify any casualties that arrived at a military treatment facility with urological-based injuries. The found that the registry contained 25,897 adult casualties, of which 7.2% sustained urological injuries.1

The median age for injury was 25, and explosive injuries (64%) and firearms (27%) were the primary causes. Most patients survived until hospital discharge (94%). The authors pointed out that the most frequently injured organs were the scrotum (60%), testes (53%), penis (30%), and kidneys (30%).

“The incidence of genitourinary trauma persistently increased for both military and civilian personnel as the U.S. remained actively engaged in major military conflicts during this period,” the study concluded. “Patients with genitourinary trauma in this data set were often associated with high injury severity scores and required an increased number of immediate and long-term resources for survival and rehabilitation.”

The injuries weren’t just immediate and physical, however. In 2014, the Bob Woodruff Foundation convened a conference examining how combat injuries affect intimacy and family planning, and many nonprofits have offered free or discounted cryopreservation services to some servicemembers in the interim. Until now, however, deploying servicemembers who wanted to bank sperm or eggs as a hedge against combat injury or prolonged separation have had to pay for it themselves, and some military families have described going to considerable lengths, including seeking emergency cryopreservation after a servicemember was critically injured, to maintain their options to have children.

Whether the new benefit becomes permanent will likely hinge on how the demonstration project affects retention. Beyond tracking cost and participation, the Pentagon has said it wants to understand whether offering the benefit affects how troops and their families view deployments and long separations, a question that goes to the heart of recruitment and retention pressures the services have faced in recent years. For now, the reimbursement applies only for the length of the three-year pilot, though the notice leaves open the possibility that the department could extend it through a subsequent Federal Register notice.

Enforcement actions and official statements In addition, under the Medicare Advantage (MA) Program, also known as Medicare Part C, Medicare beneficiaries may opt out of traditional Medicare and enroll in private health plans offered by insurance companies known as Medicare Advantage Organizations.

text:
AIDS Healthcare Foundation, a non-profit organization based in Los Angeles, California, has agreed to pay $1.44 million to resolve allegations that it violated the False Claims Act by submitting or failing to delete false or invalid diagnosis codes in order to increase payments that it received from the Medicare Advantage program. “The government relies on Medicare Advantage participants to submit accurate, substantiated diagnosis codes that are adequately documented in a medical record to ensure proper payment,” said Assistant Attorney General Brett A. Shumate of the Justice Department’s Civil Division.

Key details of the case

“The Justice Department will continue to protect the public fisc and hold accountable those who receive inflated payments by knowingly providing or failing to correct false information.”. “The integrity of our federal healthcare programs, including Medicare Advantage, must be preserved,” said First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli for the Central District of California.

Moreover, “We will not tolerate companies undermining the interests of Medicare patients for financial gain.”. “Medicare Advantage organizations have a responsibility to ensure the accuracy of diagnosis codes they submit for payment. When entities fail to correct information they know is wrong, they undermine the integrity of a program millions of seniors rely on,” said Acting Deputy Inspector General for Investigations Miranda L.

Bennett of the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services Office of Inspector General (HHS‑OIG). “HHS‑OIG will continue to safeguard taxpayer funds by holding organizations accountable when their failures inflate federal payments and compromise program trust.”.

Enforcement actions and official statements

In addition, under the Medicare Advantage (MA) Program, also known as Medicare Part C, Medicare beneficiaries may opt out of traditional Medicare and enroll in private health plans offered by insurance companies known as Medicare Advantage Organizations. MAOs. The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) pays the MAOs a fixed monthly amount for each Medicare beneficiary enrolled in their plans.

CMS adjusts these monthly payments to account for various “risk” factors that affect expected health expenditures for the beneficiary. In general, CMS pays MAOs more for sicker beneficiaries expected to incur higher healthcare costs and less for healthier beneficiaries expected to incur lower costs. To calculate the payment amounts, CMS uses a health-based risk adjustment model. For complete details, refer to the official DOJ press release.

Consequently, the Hierarchical Conditions Category (HCC) model — that takes into account diagnoses reported by healthcare providers. In general, the more severe the diagnosis or costly the associated treatment, the higher the risk score and the higher the corresponding payments to the MAO. Diagnosis codes submitted to CMS must be supported by the beneficiaries’ medical records and be accurate, complete.

Truthful, based on the best knowledge, information, and belief of the MAO making the submission. AIDS Healthcare Foundation (AHF) provides care and services to HIV patients in the United States and other countries. AHF’s Managed Care Division (doing business as Positive Healthcare Partners) operated special needs MA plans for Medicare beneficiaries who have HIV and lived in Florida, Georgia. For related coverage, see Kevin Curry convicted in $26 million TRICARE fraud and kickback scheme.

California. The settlement announced today resolves allegations that, for payment years 2017 to 2023, AHF failed to timely investigate and delete diagnosis codes that were either inaccurate or not documented in medical records. Beginning in around 2017, AHF’s risk adjustment coders conducted chart reviews to identify inaccurate or unsupported diagnosis codes for deletion.

As part of this process, AHF’s risk adjustment coders maintained “Delete Research” spreadsheets. Listed diagnosis codes they identified as potentially lacking support in the medical record but needing further research. Although AHF knew that it was required to investigate and delete inaccurate and unsupported diagnosis codes within 60 days, AHF failed to timely investigate and delete the codes. For related coverage, see Independence Blue Cross (IBX) to Pay $22.5 Million to Resolve False Claims Act Allegations.

At the same time, aHF did not delete most of the inaccurate or unsupported diagnosis codes in the “Delete Research” spreadsheets until 2024 or 2025. Well after AHF was on notice that the codes potentially lacked support and only after being notified of the United States’ investigation. The United States further alleges that, for payment year 2017, AHF knowingly submitted diagnosis codes for HIV (ICD-10 B20) where the diagnosis was not documented in any medical record for a face-to-face visit, in violation of CMS requirements that all diagnosis code submissions must be documented as a result of a face-to-face visit.

In particular, the civil settlement resolves claims brought under the qui tam or whistleblower provisions of the False Claims Act by Donna Irons, a former risk adjustment coder at AHF. Under the qui tam provisions, a private party can file an action on behalf of the United States and receive a portion of any recovery. The qui tam case is captioned United States ex rel.

Furthermore, aIDS Healthcare Foundation d/b/a Positive Healthcare Partners, Civil Action No. 23-cv-2160 (C.D. Irons will receive $259,200 as her share of the federal recovery. AHF received credit under the Department of Justice’s guidelines for taking disclosure, cooperation.

Investigation and prosecution details

Remediation into account in False Claims Act resolutions, Justice Manual § 4-4.112. In addition to cooperating in the government’s investigation and enhancing its compliance program, AHF proactively remediated its conduct during the course of Department’s investigation by submitting deletes for diagnosis codes that, based on review of medical records, were not supported. The resolution obtained in this matter was the result of a coordinated effort between the Justice Department’s Civil Division, Commercial Litigation Branch, Fraud Section and the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Central District of California, with assistance from the Department of Health and Human Services, Office of Inspector General.

text:
Command Hospital (Eastern Command), Kolkata, has successfully administered India’s indigenous CAR-T cell therapy, NexCAR19, to a 39-year-old serving soldier suffering from relapsed/refractory B-cell Acute Lymphoblastic Leukaemia (B-cell ALL), in what the Eastern Command described as a landmark achievement for military healthcare.

The treatment, carried out under the aegis of Eastern Command, is being seen as a notable step in the Armed Forces’ use of advanced medical technology to treat complex blood cancers among serving personnel. It also adds to the range of specialised cancer care available within the military health system.

NexCAR19 is India’s first indigenous CAR-T cell therapy. It was developed through a collaboration between IIT Bombay, Tata Memorial Centre and biotechnology start-up ImmunoACT. The therapy has been positioned as a more affordable and accessible immunotherapy option for blood cancers, including leukaemia and lymphoma.

CAR-T cell therapy works by taking a patient’s own T-cells and genetically modifying them with Chimeric Antigen Receptors, or CARs, so that they can recognise and attack cancer cells expressing the CD19 protein. The process involves collecting T-cells from the patient, engineering them in the laboratory, and then reinfusing the modified cells back into the body. Once administered, these cells are designed to identify and destroy the targeted cancer cells.

According to the information provided, NexCAR19 uses a humanised product configuration rather than murine, or mouse-derived, components. This is associated with a lower risk of severe neurological side effects. The therapy is regarded as an important option for patients with relapsed or refractory blood cancers who have exhausted conventional treatment options.

The cost of NexCAR19 is reported to be about one-tenth of comparable CAR-T therapies available in Western countries, making it one of the more affordable such treatments globally. Command Hospitals across India are among the institutions authorised to administer the therapy.

Eastern Command described the successful administration of the therapy to the soldier as a “landmark achievement”, saying it reflects clinical excellence, innovation and a commitment to providing cutting-edge, patient-centric healthcare to the Indian Armed Forces. The development also highlights the Army medical establishment’s efforts to adopt advanced medical technologies for serving personnel and their dependants.

The Kolkata achievement follows another recent CAR-T therapy milestone within the military healthcare network. In September, Command Hospital (Western Command), Chandimandir, administered its first CAR-T cell therapy to a 16-year-old patient diagnosed with B-cell Acute Lymphoblastic Leukaemia.

With the successful use of NexCAR19 at Command Hospital Kolkata, the Armed Forces healthcare system has added another advanced treatment capability for blood cancer patients, while also demonstrating the application of an indigenous medical technology in the treatment of a serving soldier with relapsed/refractory B-cell ALL.

title: Where USU Is Going: A Strategic Plan Built for a Fight Without a Golden Hour
description:
USU's 2026-2029 strategic plan rebuilds military medicine education, research, and partnerships for a fight without a Golden Hour.
The USU Strategic Plan calls for every USU student to demonstrate proficiency in validated combat skills by fiscal 2028.
The Uniformed Services University of the Health Sciences (USU) has adopted a strategic plan for 2026 through 2029 that starts from a harder assumption: In the next fight, that hour may not exist.
The plan sets 100% adoption by fiscal 2028, alongside a 40% increase in the share of USU's workforce proficient with AI.
USU will restructure its administration around the Office of the Provost, with 15% faster administrative processing by fiscal 2028.
text:
USU's 2026-2029 strategic plan rebuilds military medicine education, research, and partnerships for a fight without a Golden Hour.

USU students move a simulated casualty onto a litter during the university's Gunpowder field exercise. The USU Strategic Plan calls for every USU student to demonstrate proficiency in validated combat skills by fiscal 2028. (Photo credit: Tom Balfour, USU)

For most of the past two decades, a Service member wounded in combat could expect to reach a surgeon within an hour. Military medicine came to call it the Golden Hour. The Uniformed Services University of the Health Sciences (USU) has adopted a strategic plan for 2026 through 2029 that starts from a harder assumption: In the next fight, that hour may not exist.

USU President Dr. Jonathan Woodson signed the plan July 1. It commits USU to becoming a fully digital-first institution by 2029 and, in the plan's own words, "a high-acuity readiness and force generation platform" for the healthcare providers and leaders who care for the warfighter. Seven priorities carry that commitment: curriculum reform, digital transformation, strategic partnerships, campus infrastructure, financial stability, administrative restructuring, and a philanthropy foundation.

The plan is nested inside the broader direction of the Department of War (DoW). It answers the 2026 National Defense Strategy and the Assistant Secretary of War for Health Affairs' 2026 Military Health System Optimization mandates, and it aligns every USU activity with the five domains of change those mandates set out: readiness, funding stability, benefit modernization, integrated training, and structural optimization.

Woodson has framed the seven priorities as one design rather than seven projects, each depending on the others to work. "These priorities are united by a single purpose: ensuring that USU continues to provide the Military Health System with the highly skilled health professionals, innovative research, and operational expertise needed to support a medically ready force," he wrote in the letter releasing the plan.

“The advantage of USU is not found in any one of these priorities by itself,” Woodson said. “It comes from what happens when they work together. When we align how we educate, how we conduct research, how we use technology, how we partner, and how we prepare our people for the realities they will face, we create capabilities that are greater than the sum of their parts. That gives the Department of War a unique national resource, strengthens the advantage we share with our allies, and gives every USU graduate the knowledge, judgment, and experience to contribute in ways that few other health professionals can.”

The USU Strategic Plan 2026-2029, signed by President Dr. Jonathan Woodson July 1, sets seven priorities for the university. (USU Graphic)

The Battlefield the Plan Assumes

The plan opens with why it exists. The national security environment, it says, has shifted from counterinsurgency to large-scale combat operations, meaning sustained fighting between the regular forces of major powers. Four features of that fight shape everything that follows.

The first two features that shape the current landscape are about time. Adversary weapons strike farther and faster, widening the battlefield and compressing the time medical teams have to respond. Where an adversary can contest the airspace, evacuation by helicopter is no longer reliable.

The Golden Hour gives way to prolonged field care, the practice of holding and treating a casualty for hours or days in a hardened, dispersed, or underground position, often alongside allied medical teams.

A third feature is about people. The plan names the "Walker Dip," a term for the loss of combat medical expertise between wars, as a standing vulnerability. Clinicians who learned to treat blast and gunshot wounds in Iraq and Afghanistan are leaving the force, and their knowledge does not stay in the system on its own.

The fourth has no front line at all. Cyberattacks on hospital systems, synthetic biological weapons, and attacks aimed at cognition all threaten military medicine without a shot fired at a medical unit.

Educating a Provider for a Different Casualty

The curriculum is where the plan first reaches a student, and it is the priority that most directly answers that battlefield. USU will modernize what it teaches around large-scale combat operations, prolonged field care, and contested environments, so that every graduate leaves with the foundational skills a high-acuity fight demands.

Those include managing disease and non-battle injuries, the illnesses and accidents that take Service members off the line without enemy contact.

By fiscal 2028, the plan calls for 100% of students to demonstrate proficiency in validated combat knowledge, skills, and abilities examinations and to hold Joint Medical Role certifications. Those certifications confirm that a provider can function at a defined level of battlefield care, whichever service runs the facility.

The classes will grow with the content. The plan expands the F. Edward Hébert School of Medicine to an annual class of 200 students, increases enrollment at the Daniel K. Inouye Graduate School of Nursing by 10%, and expands College of Allied Health Sciences programs by 50%. USU also expects new responsibilities under the Secretary of War's Project Patriot Pipeline, a DoW-wide workforce development effort, including career pathways into health professions for DoW civilians and military spouses.

Woodson has described the result as a graduate whose education was re-examined as the fight changed rather than fixed at the moment of enrollment.

“A USU graduate leaves here with more than the clinical knowledge required to practice medicine,” Woodson said. “They understand what it means to care for patients when resources are limited, when evacuation may not be immediate, when the environment is changing, and when the consequences of a decision can extend well beyond the patient in front of them. That experience stays with them throughout their careers. Whether they are treating a Service member in a field hospital, leading a military medical team, responding to a crisis at home, or caring for patients in a civilian setting, they bring a perspective shaped by service, operational medicine, and the responsibility to care for others under the most demanding circumstances.”

A Digital-First University

Vision 2029 commits USU to lead the Military Health System in adopting artificial intelligence (AI), robotics, and predictive analytics. Its clearest near-term target is universal digital credentialing, one verified record of a provider's qualifications that follows them anywhere in the system. The plan sets 100% adoption by fiscal 2028, alongside a 40% increase in the share of USU's workforce proficient with AI.

On campus, the shift is already visible in the classroom, where USU introduced a web app that guides students through ethical AI use at every stage of a research project. Woodson has pointed to students using AI to tailor their own coursework as the nearest example of what a digital-first university looks like in practice.

USU President Dr. Jonathan Woodson and Air Marshal Clare Walton, Chief of Defence Medical for the UK, shake hands after signing a Memorandum of Understanding expanding military medical collaboration between the two nations, July 2, in London. (Photo credit: MOD Crown Copyright)

Partners Who Will Fight Together

The plan assumes American medical teams will operate alongside allied and partner forces in the next conflict, and it treats that coalition work as a capability to build now. It sets a target of two or more international academic hubs by fiscal 2028 to strengthen coalition medical readiness, along with at least five joint education or research products a year.

Within the United States, it directs USU to invest in top-tier academic and industry partners to co-create combat-relevant innovation with capabilities such as biomedical engineering.

Abroad, the work has a recent example. In July, USU and the UK Defence Medical Command signed a memorandum of understanding in London expanding their collaboration in military medical education, research, and training. Woodson framed the agreement as preparation for a shared fight.

"The United States and the United Kingdom have long stood shoulder to shoulder in military operations around the world," Woodson said at the signing. "Preparing the next generation of military healthcare professionals together builds on that legacy and ensures our forces remain ready to meet the evolving challenges of military medicine."

Allied medical services train to their own standards and doctrine, and Woodson has described a concept for reconciling them before a conflict does: a simulated medical battle lab where allied and partner medical forces would work through the friction points of operating together in rehearsal.

“Interoperability cannot be something we discover for the first time in a crisis,” Woodson said. “Our allies and partners may arrive with different medical systems, different equipment, different terminology, and different ways of organizing care. The battle lab gives us a place to identify those differences, work through them together, and build the habits and relationships that allow us to function as one medical team when it matters. The goal is not to make everyone identical. It is to make sure that when our forces have to care for patients together, we already know how to do it.”

The Work That Holds It Up

Four priorities make the first three possible. The plan directs USU to execute its Facilities Master Plan and IT Master Plan to arrest the deterioration of its physical plant and protect the accreditation that lets the classes grow. All Phase 1 modernized Armed Forces Radiobiology Research Institute and high-acuity simulation research facilities are to be certified by fiscal 2028.

Research positions move off short-term grants and onto the DoW's programmed budget, a 15% increase in the share of hard-funded positions by fiscal 2028. The reason is that research on surviving a battlefield injury runs longer than any single grant. That research is pointed toward survivability, including medical countermeasures for chemical, biological, radiological, and nuclear threats.

USU will restructure its administration around the Office of the Provost, with 15% faster administrative processing by fiscal 2028.

The plan also calls for a philanthropy foundation and alumni outreach program, with its charter finalized by fiscal 2028 charter finalized by fiscal 2028, to provide students with a margin of excellence beyond what USU’s federal appropriations can provide.

What the Plan Is Measured Against

Each school, center, and office at USU will translate the plan into its own objectives and key results, tracked against the 2029 vision. Woodson wrote that its success depends on every member of the community considering how their own work contributes.

The plan states the standard plainly. Medical success on the next battlefield "is measured solely by the survivability of the American Warfighter." Every priority above is an argument about one moment. A USU-educated provider is working in a hardened aid station with no evacuation available, keeping a wounded Service member alive for a day or more until transport is possible. The plan is a bet that they will be ready.

USU News will follow the plan over the coming year, with reporting on each priority and on the schools, centers, and people carrying the work.

If your work involves supporting veterans, please know how much I—and many others who served —appreciate it. Every holiday, I make a point to call the 988 crisis line operators to express my gratitude for their dedication to our community. My own military service spanned from 1969 to 1972, including a tour in Vietnam in 1970 as an 18-year-old infantry soldier. Navigating those years was immensely difficult, especially without resources like 988, which was not established until around 2007.

Military suicide has been a long-standing tragedy across generations. During World War II, my father and uncles observed service members taking their own lives. Later, throughout the active Vietnam War period from 1964 to 1975, 1,500 military personnel committed suicide while in Vietnam—including a young service member I personally found in November 1970. Out of the 9.7 million military members who served during that era—2.7 million of whom were deployed to Vietnam—it is estimated that more than 94,000 Vietnam veterans ultimately died by suicide.

text:
The online portal used by TRICARE beneficiaries to access health records from military hospitals and clinics will move to a new login system before the end of the year, though a planned September changeover did not take place.

The MHS GENESIS Patient Portal will move from the DS Logon system to myAuth, a changeover already made by TRICARE contractors in the East and West regions, the Pentagon’s ID Card Office Online, and other platforms. The MHS GENESIS change will only affect those who receive care at military treatment facilities (MTFs).

A TRICARE.mil announcement originally stated the MHS GENESIS changeover would take place Sept. 23. An updated announcement offers no date for the changeover and says the portal “is fully accessible via DS Logon or Common Access Card [CAC].” TRICARE officials did not announce a reason for the update.

[RELATED: Congress Presses Oracle for Answers on VA’s $17 Billion Health Record Increase]

The MHS GENESIS patient portal login page link included in the release retained DS Logon access options as of Oct. 5, while patient portal links from other official sites, such as MyArmyBenefits, pointed to a myAuth login page as of that date.

About myAuth

Users with a DS Logon account or a CAC can use those credentials to create a myAuth account. Once created, users can log in using their CAC, the Okta Verify app, or their username and password plus a “secure multi-factor authentication method,” according to the TRICARE announcement – generally a one-time passcode received via email.

(Beneficiaries who access health care data at their TRICARE contractor websites via other login methods – usually via an email registered in the Defense Enrollment Eligibility Reporting System (DEERS) – can continue to log in as normal.)

The same account credentials can be used to access any site using myAuth, including milConnect, Military OneSource, and the Express Scripts TRICARE Pharmacy portal. Note: Login options other than myAuth may be available for these and other sites.

title: From Copays to Logins: Here's What's Changing for TRICARE Beneficiaries in 2027
description:
Open Season is the annual period when beneficiaries can enroll or change their enrollment in TRICARE for the next calendar year.
For dental and vision plans under the Federal Benefits Open Season (FEDVIP), Open Season ends on December 14, 2026, giving you six extra days beyond the medical deadline.
All changes made during Open Season take effect on January 1, 2027.
"The number of urgent care visits remains unlimited without referrals for TRICARE Prime enrollees for Plan CY 2027.
For Urgent Care, it’s still the same, and there are different rules depending on whether the urgent care clinic or convenience clinic is in network or not.
text:
Like all medical insurance programs, including government-run programs such as Medicare and Medicaid, TRICARE will be making its annual adjustments to its programs and coverage, including out-of-pocket costs, coverage options, program features, and how beneficiaries can access their portal online.

The tricare.mil/changes page has not been updated since July 6 of this year, but there are some things that we do know. The Defense Health Agency (DHA) has already posted those planned changes in the Federal Register, and out-of-pocket changes are linked to the federal COLA and Consumer Price Index.

Open Season is the annual period when beneficiaries can enroll or change their enrollment in TRICARE for the next calendar year. This year, Open Season runs from November 9 through December 8, 2026, for medical plans. For dental and vision plans under the Federal Benefits Open Season (FEDVIP), Open Season ends on December 14, 2026, giving you six extra days beyond the medical deadline. All changes made during Open Season take effect on January 1, 2027. If you don't make any changes, then your coverage remains the same (of course with any adjustments to cost-sharing). Beneficiaries can check or update their information on DEERS.

How Cost Is Changing for FY2027

First, cost increases almost always follow the cost-of-living adjustment (COLA), which is governed under federal law and is automatic. Cost changes really only affect those who are not enrolled in TRICARE Prime and receive most of their care at military treatment facilities (MTF).

For all others, they can expect their enrollment fees, premiums, caps, deductibles, and co-pays to go up commensurate with the approved federal COLA. The COLA for retired pay (and Social Security) is automatic and is based on the change in the Consumer Price Index - Wages.

In 2025, that adjustment was 2.5%, and in 2026 it was slightly higher at 2.8%. We can expect TRICARE out-of-pocket expenses to increase by roughly the same percentage in FY2027. There is one exception: pharmacy out-of-pocket expenses, which remain unchanged going into the next calendar year.

TRICARE’s Annual Announcements

There are program features that the DHA adjusts each year. They range from adding features, adjustments to eligibility, and changes to service areas. Two things are not changing: Prime Service Areas remain the same, and Urgent Care visits still do not require a referral.

"The number of urgent care visits remains unlimited without referrals for TRICARE Prime enrollees for Plan CY 2027. Beneficiaries may receive urgent care from TRICARE-authorized urgent care centers (UCCs) and convenience clinics (CCs), either network or non-network, without a referral," explained the Federal Register Notice.

Prime Service Areas remaining unchanged means that if you are enrolled in Prime, your MTF will likely remain the same. For Urgent Care, it’s still the same, and there are different rules depending on whether the urgent care clinic or convenience clinic is in network or not.

Beneficiaries seeing out-of-network providers in urgent care or convenience care clinics can expect to pay co-pays and deductibles. Active duty service members have different rules, so it's always best to ask the MTF Patient Advocate well beforehand if possible.

What’s Extended in 2027

TRICARE-eligible beneficiaries, including active duty, family members, and retirees and their family members, may elect to participate in a "Competitive Plans Demonstration.”

The test program is limited to certain zip codes in the metro Atlanta, Georgia, and Tampa, Florida, areas. TRICARE beneficiaries in those areas who enroll will receive their care solely through CareSource Military & Veterans. According to their website, CareSource is a “national, nonprofit managed care organization serving over 2 million members in 12 states,” and it already provides health care via Medicaid and other government-sponsored healthcare programs.

Beneficiaries in the Atlanta and Tampa areas can check to see if they are eligible using TRICARE’s Plan Finder.

Also new in 2027 is a five-year nationwide demonstration for how Pre-Hospital Blood Transfusions (PHBT) are paid and reimbursed. Pre-Hospital Blood Transfusion is a practice pioneered on the battlefield and has a proven track record of saving trauma patients' lives. Initial DHA analysis led to the conclusion that TRICARE beneficiaries were bearing more of the cost of this procedure than intended, and researchers found that the cost to the patient could be an average of around $237 per unit of blood given by first responders. The DHA plan is to continue evaluating costs and determine the appropriate reimbursement, subject to co-pays and deductibles, of course.

Finally, the Childbirth and Breastfeeding Support Demonstration has been extended for five more years. This means beneficiaries may still access certified labor doulas, lactation consultants, and lactation counselors until December 31, 2031.

Program and Benefit Changes

Active duty family members enrolled in TRICARE Prime Remote, who are more than 50 miles or a one-hour drive from their MTF pharmacy, will no longer be charged a co-pay for using a local pharmacy. This is a significant time and money saver for military families.

A host of new treatments have now been added to TRICARE’s approved list. They include the Optune (TM) Tumor Treating Fields Device, an ablative fractional laser for the treatment of scars resulting from burns and other trauma, as well as liver transplant for metastatic colorectal cancer, among others. The full list of newly approved procedures and devices can be found here. There is also new provisional coverage for “vertebral body tethering,” an alternative to spinal fusion therapy for treating adolescent scoliosis.

One treatment has already been terminated. Transcutaneous Electrical Nerve Stimulation (TENS) devices were excluded from coverage effective July 1, 2026, for all conditions except acute post-operative pain.

Lastly, just like the VA, TRICARE is transitioning from DS-LOGON as the common authentication to myAuth. DS-LOGON shut down completely on September 30, 2026. You can create a myAuth login from any login page (VA.gov, TRICARE.mil, etc.).

Beneficiaries can link their current DS-LOGON account if they create their new myAuth credentials before the end of September. Multifactor Authentication (MFA) is required, and those without a CAC will be required to use the Okta app on their phone or PC. If you have questions, the Defense Manpower Data Center (DMDC) help desk is available at 800-368-3665.

Keeping up with changes in TRICARE, no matter whether you’re on active duty, a retiree, or a family member, will ensure you can make the most of your plan and your coverage.

text:
Download logo

Advances in specialised medical care are strengthening the Kenya Defence Forces (KDF) health system, expanding access to complex treatment while reducing the need to refer patients to external healthcare facilities.

Defence Forces Memorial Hospital (DFMH) has achieved a major medical milestone after successfully conducting its first red blood cell exchange using the newly acquired Spectra Optia® apheresis system.

The procedure, performed at the hospital’s Renal Unit on 2 October 2026, involved a 15-year-old female patient living with sickle cell disease. Its successful completion marks an important expansion of DFMH’s capacity to manage complex blood disorders through specialised and technology-enabled care.

Apheresis is an advanced blood-processing procedure that selectively separates specific components of a patient’s blood while returning the remaining components to the body. The technology enables clinicians to undertake specialised therapeutic procedures tailored to particular medical conditions.

During a red blood cell exchange, abnormal or sickled red blood cells are removed from the patient’s circulation and replaced with compatible donor red blood cells. This reduces the proportion of sickled cells in the bloodstream and can form part of specialised management for patients with sickle cell disease.

The introduction of the capability at DFMH represents more than the successful completion of a single procedure. It expands the hospital’s ability to provide specialised haematological interventions within the KDF healthcare system, enabling eligible patients who require red blood cell exchange to access the service at the facility.

The acquisition of the Spectra Optia® system also provides a platform for the progressive development of other therapeutic apheresis procedures and advanced transfusion support.

As the service develops, it is expected to strengthen multidisciplinary management of patients with complex haematological and other conditions requiring specialised blood-component therapy.

For KDF personnel, their families and other eligible beneficiaries, the new capability enhances access to advanced medical treatment while strengthening continuity of care within the military health system.

The milestone demonstrates DFMH’s continued advancement as a specialised referral facility and highlights the role of modern medical technology, skilled healthcare professionals and sustained capability development in improving patient outcomes.

text:
A federal jury has found a 64-year-old Texas man guilty of illegally billing Tricare for millions of dollars in services that were medically unnecessary or never delivered to patients at clinics in Texas and Florida, according to the Justice Department.

Kevin D. Curry, 64, of Frisco, Texas, directed employees at the three clinics he operated to falsify patient records to support $26 million in medical claims that were then submitted to the military insurance program, the Department of Justice said.

Curry was convicted on Sept. 24 in U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Texas on multiple counts of health care fraud, paying illegal kickbacks and money laundering, according to the DOJ.

He used actual doctors’ credentials without their knowledge to falsify the billings for a noninvasive procedure called transcranial magnetic stimulation therapy for treatment of major depressive and mood disorders, according to court documents.

Curry “offered and paid over $5.5 million in kickbacks to convince active-duty service members, veterans and their family members to consent to TMS therapy they did not qualify for and, in many instances, did not receive,” the DOJ said in a news release.

The medical services were “not provided at all, not provided as represented, medically unnecessary and/or induced by illegal kickbacks and bribes,” court documents said.

Curry then used the Tricare reimbursements to fund a lavish lifestyle, including a gold-plated Tesla Cybertruck, stays at luxury hotels, and casino parties that he hosted, the DOJ said.

“This defendant exploited a critical health care program serving active-duty service members and their families, diverting taxpayer dollars to bankroll personal luxuries,” said Colin McDonald, assistant attorney general at the DOJ’s fraud enforcement division.

The jury convicted Curry on three counts of health care fraud, three counts of offering and paying illegal health care kickbacks, and three counts of engaging in monetary transactions in criminally derived property, according to the DOJ.

Curry faces up to 10 years in federal prison for each of the nine counts. He is scheduled to be sentenced at a later date.

Curry, who is licensed as a mental health counselor, owned Acuity mental health clinics in Plano and Fort Worth, Texas, and in Fort Walton Beach, Fla.

Curry operated the clinics from September 2022 through December 2025, court documents said. Tricare paid out $17 million to Acuity clinics, the DOJ said.

Tricare is the military’s insurance program covering active duty personnel, National Guard and Reserve members, retirees, dependents and their survivors.

SOAA is actively advocating against state-level pharmacy benefit manager (PBM) reforms that could disrupt critical prescription access.
For people who depend on regular prescriptions, changes to pharmacy access can raise immediate questions about travel, cost, and continuity of care.

text: Current pharmacy access and TRICARE reform proposals could harm Veterans and military families. SOAA is actively advocating against state-level pharmacy benefit manager (PBM) reforms that could disrupt critical prescription access. For people who depend on regular prescriptions, changes to pharmacy access can raise immediate questions about travel, cost, and continuity of care. Our initial member survey asked how respondents would be affected if the pharmacy they use most often closed. More than 55% said the impact would be moderate or substantial. Nearly 70% identified convenient, affordable prescriptions as a major concern for themselves or their families. Rural respondents described having fewer nearby alternatives, while others said home delivery would shield them from the effects of a local closure. One respondent said their “family would be devastated” by a pharmacy closure. Another described depending on a monthly glaucoma prescription “to keep [their] eyes from going blind.” Others pointed to out-of-stock medications and co-pays as more immediate concerns. The responses make clear why veterans’ experiences belong in this policy conversation. Our initial findings: https://lnkd.in/gfrjmcF5

title: Congress Heads Home, But MOAA's NDAA Push Continues
description:
The Senate Armed Services Committee (SASC) reported its version (S. 4784) in June, but it has yet to pass the full chamber.
House and Senate members are working through their differences as part of an informal process between the two chambers rather than the traditional conference committee process.
Members of MOAA’s government relations team highlighted several key provisions that have a path forward in the NDAA and that we hope to see included in the final legislation.
MOAA also recently joined The Military Coalition (TMC) in a letter urging congressional leaders to preserve and advance a broad range of provisions in the final NDAA.
This legislation was not included in either the House or Senate versions of the FY 2027 NDAA but remains a top TMC priority.
text:
While lawmakers will not return to Washington until after the midterm elections, MOAA will continue pressing Congress to advance critical priorities for servicemembers, retirees, their families, and survivors as part of must-pass defense legislation.

With the FY 2027 National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA) entering the final stages of the legislative process, MOAA is maintaining a consistent presence on Capitol Hill to ensure key provisions remain in the final bill and to improve legislative language to achieve the intended outcomes.

The House passed its version of the bill (H.R. 8800) on July 22. The Senate Armed Services Committee (SASC) reported its version (S. 4784) in June, but it has yet to pass the full chamber. House and Senate members are working through their differences as part of an informal process between the two chambers rather than the traditional conference committee process.

[LEARN MORE: MOAA’s NDAA Priorities]

MOAA joined a group of military and veterans service organizations Sept. 23 for a meeting with SASC professional staff as the committee prepares to reconcile differences between the House and Senate bills. Members of MOAA’s government relations team highlighted several key provisions that have a path forward in the NDAA and that we hope to see included in the final legislation. The team also recommended targeted changes to legislative language on certain provisions to better align the final language with the needs of the military and veteran communities.

MOAA also recently joined The Military Coalition (TMC) in a letter urging congressional leaders to preserve and advance a broad range of provisions in the final NDAA.

[READ THE LETTER]

TMC represents a combined 5.5 million-plus members. MOAA co-chairs the coalition and many of its committees.

In its letter to armed services committee leaders in both chambers, TMC thanked the lawmakers for their bipartisan work on the NDAA and noted support for numerous provisions related to health care access, reserve component benefits, military family housing safety, Military Retirement Fund parity for the U.S. Public Health Service and NOAA, and expanded child care options.

TMC also noted its continued support for the Major Richard Star Act. This legislation was not included in either the House or Senate versions of the FY 2027 NDAA but remains a top TMC priority.

title: DOGE's claim of $110B in savings was vastly inflated and riddled with errors: GAO
description:
A new review by the U.S. Government Accountability Office found the site's claim of $110 billion in taxpayer savings was vastly inflated and unreliable.
The report found DOGE could not provide enough information to verify 96% of its reported savings from canceled grants.
According to the report, $27.4 billion in claimed savings was never executed, and DOGE did not provide identifying information for another $7.2 billion in claimed savings.

text:
When Elon Musk's Department of Government Efficiency launched its effort to slash federal spending last year, it also created a website to show how much money it said it was saving taxpayers.

A new review by the U.S. Government Accountability Office found the site's claim of $110 billion in taxpayer savings was vastly inflated and unreliable.

The report found DOGE could not provide enough information to verify 96% of its reported savings from canceled grants.

Despite its pledge of transparency, the report found DOGE did not use its stated methodology to calculate about half of the savings it reported.

“Because U.S. DOGE Service officials did not respond to requests for information, GAO could not determine the reasons why DOGE did not disclose data quality issues and limitations when the website first went live or at any time since then,” the report said.

The report also found DOGE failed to terminate some of the contracts it claimed to have canceled. According to the report, $27.4 billion in claimed savings was never executed, and DOGE did not provide identifying information for another $7.2 billion in claimed savings.

DOGE also claimed $1.7 billion in savings from an IT services contract for the Defense Department's Defense Health Agency, but the report said no changes were ever made.

The report also said DOGE claimed savings from millions of dollars in leases that had already been identified for termination.

Musk has since left DOGE. ABC News reached out to Musk and the White House for comment but did not immediately receive a response.

Although DOGE formally ended on July 4, its "Wall of Receipts" remains online, claiming a total of $215 billion in taxpayer savings.

Inadequate prescription drug reimbursement, PBM contracts, below-cost payments, and shrinking pharmacy margins are creating serious problems across community and retail pharmacy. text:
Authored by Austin Campbell via Task & Purpose,

Millions of dollars spent on casino-themed parties, expensive hotels and a gold-plated Cybertruck. It sounds like the spending spree of a character from The Wolf of Wall Street. Instead, federal prosecutors say the absurd spending was financed by a 64-year-old mental health clinic owner named Kevin Darnell Curry.

Curry, who owned and operated Acuity TMS of Plano, Acuity TMS of Fort Worth and Emerald Coast TMS of Fort Walton Beach, was convicted of submitting roughly $26 million in fraudulent claims to TRICARE, which paid out approximately $17 million.

These clinics, which offered transcranial magnetic stimulation or TMS, operated in areas with substantial military populations. His Fort Walton Beach clinic sat in the same Florida Panhandle military community as Eglin Air Force Base and Hurlburt Field, while his Fort Worth operation was near Naval Air Station Joint Reserve Base Fort Worth. A third clinic operated in Plano, north of Dallas, Texas.

The scheme involved an unknown number of active duty service members, veterans and military family members covered by TRICARE, though the indictment did not identify where they lived or which installations, if any, the active-duty beneficiaries were assigned to. Curry falsely presented himself as a medical doctor, using fake credentials to convince service members and families to sign up for the treatment.

Curry was convicted of three counts of health care fraud, three counts of offering and paying illegal health care kickbacks and three counts of engaging in monetary transactions in criminally derived property. Federal authorities previously seized approximately $200,000 in assets connected to Curry's case, including $136,022 in cash and the gold-plated Cybertruck, according to the Justice Department.

Prosecutors say Curry recruited TRICARE beneficiaries through illegal kickbacks and bribes to receive TMS, then billed TRICARE for treatments that weren't provided, weren't provided as represented or for which patients did not qualify.

TMS is a noninvasive treatment that uses magnetic pulses to stimulate nerve cells in areas of the brain involved in depression. TRICARE covers the treatment for some patients with major depressive disorder when other treatments have failed.

To qualify, patients generally had to have tried at least two antidepressants from different drug classes without success and undergone evidence-based psychotherapy that also failed to adequately treat their depression, according to the indictment.

Prosecutors say some of Curry's patients did not meet those requirements. His clinics allegedly submitted false information about beneficiaries' treatment histories to obtain authorization from TRICARE, including records claiming patients had unsuccessfully tried medications they had not actually taken.

The scheme turned military beneficiaries into a source of millions of dollars in fraudulent TRICARE payments and unfolded inside a military health system that has simultaneously been trying to convince service members they can trust it enough to seek mental health care.

Despite the benefits of treatment, an estimated 60% to 70% of military personnel experiencing mental health problems do not seek mental health services, according to the Defense Department's Psychological Health Center of Excellence.

The Pentagon attributes that gap to a range of barriers, including stigma and concerns about how seeking treatment could affect a service member's career.

Those concerns can include fears about being viewed as weak, being treated differently by military leadership or losing the confidence of others in their unit.

It remains unclear how much of the approximately $17 million paid by TRICARE has been recovered.

Curry is scheduled to be sentenced at a later date and faces up to 10 years in prison on each count.
